text: Jean François Chazy (15 August 1882, Villefranche-sur-Saône – 9 March 1955, Paris) was a French mathematician and astronomer. He was the son of a small provincial manufacturer and studied mathematics at the École Normale Supérieure, completing the agrégation in 1905. He earned his doctorate in 1910 with the thesis Équations différentielles du troisième ordre et d’ordre supérieur don't l’intégrale générale a ses points critiques fixes. In 1911, he became maître de conférences in mechanics at Grenoble and then in Lille. During World War I, he served in the artillery and gained recognition for accurately predicting the location of the German siege gun that bombarded Paris. After the war, he served as a professor at the Faculté des Sciences de Lille (which later became the Lille University of Science and Technology) and simultaneously taught at the Institut industriel du Nord (École Centrale de Lille). In 1923, he was maître de conférences at the École centrale des arts et manufactures in Paris and also served as an examiner at the École polytechnique. In 1924, he became professor of mechanics and later of celestial mechanics at the Sorbonne, where he retired in 1953 as professor emeritus. His research focused on celestial mechanics, particularly the three-body problem and the perihelion precession of Mercury's orbit, a phenomenon later explained by Albert Einstein's general relativity theory. In 1922, Chazy received the Valz Prize from the French Academy of Sciences for his work on the three-body problem. He was an Invited Speaker of the International Congress of Mathematicians (ICM) in 1924 in Toronto and in 1928 in Bologna. In 1937, he was elected to the Académie des Sciences in the Astronomie section. He was also a member of the Romanian Academy of Sciences and the Belgian Academy of Sciences. In 1934, he served as president of the Société Mathématique de France. Since 1952, he was an official member of the Bureau des Longitudes. He was made a commander of the Légion d'honneur.
